Parallel and high-throughput topic modeling

Written by Mohammed Saqr and Sonsoles López-Pernas

Source: vignettes/articles/parallel.Rmd
parallel.Rmd

A topic model in sbert is built in three stages. Each text is encoded into an embedding by a neural model; each text is tokenized into words, which label the topics and measure their coherence; and the embeddings are clustered into topics by k-means. Encoding is by far the most expensive of the three, because it runs a transformer over every text, while tokenization and clustering are base-R operations on data already in memory. A large corpus is therefore fast to model mainly when it is encoded as few times as possible, and only then when the remaining work uses the processor cores the machine has.

Speed is worth little if it changes the answer. A setting that makes a fit faster but moves a document to another topic would make results depend on the machine they were computed on. This guide covers, in order of the time they save, reusing embeddings within and across sessions, threads and cores, and the settings that reduce the cost of encoding sentences, and for each it states whether the result can change.

library(sbert)
#> sbert 0.6.0: Sentence-BERT embeddings and topic models in R.
#>   14 pinned models (see models()); default: all-MiniLM-L6-v2.
#>   A model is downloaded only on request, once, and verified by SHA-256.

Data

Two corpora are used. The steps that need no model run on the feedback messages, whose embeddings are bundled; the steps that encode are shown on the COVID-19 abstracts and are not run, because they need a downloaded model (see models and the cache).

  • corpus: the first 600 distinct English feedback messages (translation), with their source-language text (feedback) and number of occurrences (n). Their all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings are the bundled matrix feedback_embeddings, one row per message.
  • abstracts: the covid abstracts with an abstract (Abstract).
corpus <- head(dedupe(feedback_translations, column = "translation"), 600)
abstracts <- subset(covid, Abstract != "[No abstract available]")
c(messages = nrow(corpus), abstracts = nrow(abstracts))
#>  messages abstracts 
#>       600      3847

The feedback corpus has 600 messages and the abstracts 3,847 texts.

Encode once, fit many times

topics() and compare_topics() encode the texts themselves when given a model. An analysis rarely fits one model, so the first saving is to encode once with encode() and pass the matrix as embeddings to every fit.

model <- load_model("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
embeddings <- with(abstracts, encode(Abstract, model))

model_8 <- topics(abstracts, column = "Abstract", n_topics = 8,
                  embeddings = embeddings)
model_12 <- topics(abstracts, column = "Abstract", n_topics = 12,
                   embeddings = embeddings)

Each fit still tokenizes the texts. topic_corpus() goes one step further: it stores the embeddings and the tokenized words together, so that later fits repeat neither. On the feedback messages:

prepared <- topic_corpus(corpus, column = "translation",
                         embeddings = feedback_embeddings)
prepared
#> <sbert_topic_corpus>
#>   documents: 600 
#>   embedding dimension: 384 
#>   model: precomputed embeddings 
#>   tokenization: min_token_length = 2
direct <- topics(corpus, n_topics = 6, column = "translation",
                 embeddings = feedback_embeddings)
from_corpus <- topics(prepared, n_topics = 6)
identical(as.data.frame(direct), as.data.frame(from_corpus))
#> [1] TRUE
identical(terms(direct), terms(from_corpus))
#> [1] TRUE

The prepared corpus holds 600 documents with 384-dimensional embeddings. The model fitted to it is identical to the model fitted to the raw texts, in its document table and in its terms: the corpus saves work and changes nothing. It also fixes the segmentation and tokenization settings, so a later call that asks for different ones is refused with an error rather than silently re-tokenized.

compare_topics() prepares a corpus itself, once for all the counts it compares. A topic_corpus() object is useful when several comparisons, or fits one at a time, are run on the same texts.

Reuse embeddings across sessions

encode(cache = ) writes embeddings to a file and reads them back the next time. Each text is stored under a SHA-256 digest of the text and the model’s settings, so only texts that are not yet in the file are encoded.

store <- file.path(cache_dir(), "covid_embeddings.rds")
embeddings <- with(abstracts, encode(Abstract, model, cache = store))  # encodes all
embeddings <- with(abstracts, encode(Abstract, model, cache = store))  # encodes none

Because each text has its own entry, the cache also serves a corpus that changes. If some abstracts are corrected, new ones added, rows reordered or a subset taken, only the new or changed texts are encoded. Texts repeated within one call are encoded once.

The digest covers the text exactly as the model sees it, including any prefix, and the model’s name, revision, dimension, maximum length, pooling and normalize. Change any of these and the texts are encoded again; a different model never reuses another model’s embeddings.

batch_size and sort_by_length are not part of the digest. They change which texts share a batch, which moves embeddings by about 1e-7, and including them would make the cache miss whenever the batch size changed. A cached embedding is therefore the one computed the first time, whatever the batch settings of later calls. A cache file that cannot be read, or was written for another embedding dimension, is rebuilt with a warning of class sbert_cache_rebuilt.

Threads: encoding

load_model(threads = ) sets how many threads ONNX Runtime uses to encode. Encoding is the only part of the package that uses threads. The default is one thread, which keeps runs comparable across machines.

model <- load_model("all-MiniLM-L6-v2", threads = "auto")
embeddings <- with(abstracts, encode(Abstract, model))

threads = "auto" uses the number of performance cores on Apple Silicon and half the logical cores elsewhere, at most eight. Encoding gains from threads only up to the number of performance cores; efficiency cores add contention rather than speed. The gain depends on the machine and is noisy from run to run, so a thread count is best chosen by timing a few repeated encodes of the corpus at hand. ?load_model reports the package’s own measurements, including that the embeddings were identical at every thread count measured.

Cores: tokenizing, splitting and comparing

cores is an argument of topics(), compare_topics(), topic_corpus(), coherence(), segment() and topic_gamma(). With more than one core, these functions tokenize and split documents in forked worker processes, and compare_topics() also fits its candidate numbers of topics in parallel. Forking uses parallel::mclapply(), which is available on Linux and macOS; on Windows everything runs on one core.

Tokenizing and splitting run on one core when there are fewer than 2,000 texts, because starting processes would cost more than it saves. Fitting the candidates of compare_topics() has no such threshold: each candidate is a separate k-means fit, so with cores = 2 two candidates are fitted at once even on a small corpus. The result is the same either way.

one_core <- compare_topics(prepared, n_topics = c(4, 6, 8, 10), cores = 1)
two_cores <- compare_topics(prepared, n_topics = c(4, 6, 8, 10), cores = 2)
one_core
#> <sbert_topic_sweep> 4 candidates, coherence measure: npmi
#>  n_topics coherence topic_diversity explained converged
#>         4    -0.207           0.925     0.123      TRUE
#>         6    -0.104           0.917     0.226      TRUE
#>         8    -0.118           0.900     0.243      TRUE
#>        10    -0.187           0.860     0.256      TRUE
#> 
#> Fitted models retained: fitted(x, n_topics = 6)
identical(as.data.frame(one_core), as.data.frame(two_cores))
#> [1] TRUE
identical(as.data.frame(fitted(one_core, n_topics = 8)),
          as.data.frame(fitted(two_cores, n_topics = 8)))
#> [1] TRUE

The comparison tables are identical, and so are the fitted eight-topic models taken from them. Every candidate is fitted independently and deterministically, and no random numbers are drawn in a fit, so the order in which the workers finish cannot matter.

Splitting is parallel only above 2,000 texts, so the abstracts show it.

serial <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "sentence", cores = 1))
forked <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "sentence", cores = 2))
nrow(forked)
#> [1] 35151
identical(serial, forked)
#> [1] TRUE

The 3,847 abstracts are split into 35,151 sentences on one core and, on Linux and macOS, on two worker processes, with identical results: each document is split independently and the pieces are put back in input order. On Windows both calls run on one core, and the comparison is identical trivially.

For a large corpus on Linux or macOS, the full set of cores is set once and reused.

prepared_abstracts <- topic_corpus(abstracts, column = "Abstract",
                                   embeddings = embeddings, cores = 4)
sweep <- compare_topics(prepared_abstracts, n_topics = c(6, 8, 10, 12),
                        cores = 4)

Encoding sentences efficiently

Splitting documents into sentences, as described in segmenting long documents, multiplies the number of texts to encode. Two settings reduce that cost.

sort_by_length = TRUE (in encode() and topic_gamma()) encodes texts of similar length together. Every text in a batch is padded to the length of the longest one, so a batch of mixed lengths spends much of its work on padding. The more the lengths vary, as they do for sentences and clauses, the more sorting saves. dedupe_segments = TRUE in topic_gamma() encodes each distinct segment once; the saving depends on how often segments repeat.

gamma <- with(abstracts, topic_gamma(
  model_8, Abstract,
  model = model,
  level = "sentence",
  sort_by_length = TRUE,
  dedupe_segments = TRUE,
  cores = 4
))

Both settings are off by default because they change which texts share a batch, which moves embeddings by about 1e-7. That can, rarely, move a segment that lies on the border between two topics. Once chosen, they should be kept fixed for the whole analysis.

The cheapest route is to fit the model to sentences in the first place. topics(segment = "sentence") splits, encodes and stores every sentence with its abstract, so topic_gamma() needs no further encoding:

sentence_model <- topics(abstracts, column = "Abstract", n_topics = 8,
                         segment = "sentence", max_tokens = 256,
                         model = model, cores = 4)
topic_gamma(sentence_model)

The static model

potion-base-8M is a static model: it looks up a vector for each token and averages them, with no neural network and no ONNX Runtime. Encoding is therefore far cheaper than with all-MiniLM-L6-v2, but the average ignores word order. Whether its topics are as good depends on the corpus, so the two are best compared with compare_topics() before switching.

fast <- load_model("potion-base-8M")
fast_embeddings <- with(abstracts, encode(Abstract, fast))
compare_topics(abstracts, n_topics = c(6, 8, 10, 12), column = "Abstract",
               embeddings = fast_embeddings)

Which setting for which bottleneck

  • Several models on one corpus: pass embeddings, or prepare a topic_corpus() once.
  • The same corpus in a later session, or an edited corpus: encode(cache = ).
  • Slow encoding: load_model(threads = "auto"), or the static potion-base-8M.
  • A large corpus, or many candidate counts, on Linux or macOS: cores.
  • Sentence-level models: sort_by_length = TRUE, or fit with segment = "sentence".
  • Exact reproducibility: cores and cache do not change results, and ?load_model reports none from threads; batch_size, sort_by_length and dedupe_segments can move embeddings by about 1e-7, so they are fixed once chosen. The verification guide shows how determinism is tested.
